title: Spiral galaxy NGC 300 (H-alpha band)
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 300 in hydrogen light, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-meter telescope
celestial: NGC 300 · constellation Sculptor · about 6 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Official ESO press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This view of the spiral galaxy NGC 300 was taken through a narrow filter that lets through only the red light of hydrogen atoms, known as H-alpha. It picks out clouds of glowing gas rather than the full starlight of the galaxy.

Many of those clouds owe their shapes to a population of bright young stars that switched on just a few million years ago. Their intense radiation and strong stellar winds, streams of particles flowing off their surfaces, have sculpted the surrounding gas. The radiation also strips electrons from the hydrogen, and this ionized gas forms shells, known as HII shells, that glow.
The rings visible around some of the bright stars are not real structures at all. They are caused by internal reflections inside the telescope.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (21.86 x 17.75 arcminutes) and distance (6 million light years), the frame spans roughly 38,000 × 31,000 light-years. Its light set out about 6 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image was taken with the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-meter telescope through a single H-alpha filter, which isolates the red glow of hydrogen.
understand.eye: A narrow filter shows only one color of light, so this view isolates hydrogen gas in a way the eye, which takes in all visible colors at once, cannot.
